utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Brdjanin good morning to you. Can you hear me a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I can hear you and I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. General Talic, good morning to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I can hear you in a language that I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And you may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager, Your Honours. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman along with Tania Radosavljevic and Marela Jevtovic for Mr. Brdjanin. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Appearances for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. I am Natasha Ivanovic-Fauveau. I'm assisted by Fabien Masson and I represent General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning to you, Madam Fauveau. General Talic, again, I am in duty bound to ask you whether you are happy with the situation. THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm happy with the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, any preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we might as well proceed. Call the witness, please. Ms. Korner, may I ask you how long do you expect your second part of your direct examination to last.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Probably for the next two days. I intend to take him through as many of the Sanski Most documents as I can because it's a way of dealing with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So basically we need the three -- original three documents --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If Your Honours still have the list that we provided, you will see that -- I'm going to finish off the actual events of Manjaca this morning. I hope not -- fairly quickly. Then I'm going to go into his investigations into the events of Sanski Most. That will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There are -- there are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I misguided my secretary. Let me see. Because I asked her to bring over Prosecutor's -- no. I think -- yes. Okay. I think --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's the attachments to his statement, which are the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. It's all right. I did not misguide her. I for a moment, I thought I had.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I don't think we'll get to the Sanski Most binders today, in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Judge Draganovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. May I ask you again to make the solemn declaration then, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Judge. You may sit down. And welcome back to this Tribunal. Ms. Korner for the Prosecution will resume her direct examination, her examination-in-chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: She will when she's got her earphones sorted. Sorry, Your Honour. I'm afraid I forgot to put them on. And I noticed when I was reading through Friday's transcript that there were pleas from the interpreters which I never heard because I didn't have my earphones on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It happens to me sometimes. When the debate is just English, sometimes I take them off myself. And if there is a remark or comment, I miss it. Examined by Ms. Korner: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Judge, two weeks ago or whenever it was when you stopped we were just dealing with visitors to Manjaca. And I want to try and complete the Manjaca saga quite shortly this morning. You described the various beatings, the killings, and everything that happened whilst you were there. Can I just bring it down one rung. Were there incidents where it wasn't so much a question of physical violence but in some way incidents designed to humiliate you and your fellow prisoners? You have already described one where you were made to give the three-fingered salute. Were there other incidents like that which you remember?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the arrival at the camp itself, there were many such incidents, every day. They happened all the time. There were humiliations of the people in the camps which never ceased. And this took place from when we entered the camp until the people left the camp. I could mention numerous examples of humiliations which I can remember. For example, we always had to have our heads bowed and keep our arms behind our backs from the time we entered the camp. So we weren't allowed to look at anyone. We had to look at the ground. We had to bow our heads down towards the ground. And if a military policeman noticed that someone hadn't bowed his or her head sufficiently, he would approach that person and beat that person up. He would kick that person, punch the person in the chest -- I saw this on several occasions. For example, when I was working in the kitchen and when people came to get food and they were waiting in the line and they all had to keep their heads bowed and weren't allowed to look anywhere but only at the ground. If one of those poor old people forgot what they had to do and raised their head slightly, then the policeman would approach them and beat them severely. On one occasion I was also hit in the face. I was punched in the face very -- very strongly by a policeman while returning from the kitchen -- from the place where the kitchen was located towards the -- the barn, which I was supposed to enter. And if people didn't put their hands behind their backs - this is the position they were supposed to be in -- if I may, I would stand up to show you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you pause, Judge, for a moment, because we have to describe this to get on to the note. You're bending forwards from the waist with your head bowed -- in a bowed --

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your hands behind your back.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. You may sit down, Judge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] Later on perhaps after having spent three or four months in the camp, they would introduce certain other measures. For example, if they saw that someone didn't have his arms behind his back, the policeman would order that person to crawl on the ground in the mud. They would be ordered to call in the mud from barn to barn for a distance of about 50 up to 100 metres, and they would be prostrate on the ground, and they would crawl, and they would have to get into the barn by crawling in this way. That was one form of humiliation which was present all the time. And then I can also remember permanent verbal humiliation, so to speak. They told us that we weren't a people of any kind. They said, "What do you want? Do you want a state? You're not going to have one. You'll be like the Palestinians." Then they would bring Serbian bills, and they would show them to us. They would say, "Look, we've got a state. We've got our own money." And then they would bring the number plates of vehicles, and they showed these number plates to us. They would say, "Look, we Serbs, we've got our state. We've got the Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina. You're going to be killed. All of you here in the camp are going to be killed. No one wants you. We have offered you to others, but no one wants you." But Izetbegovic, who was the Bosniak's president -- "No one wants you apart from Izetbegovic." So these were humiliations, insults that took place on a daily basis. People were insulted individually, and the collective Bosniak people was insulted. They forced us to sing songs which were Chetnik songs. These are songs which were known to be Chetnik songs in the Second World War. We had to sing these songs. The humiliations that took place in these barns where we stayed and in which the conditions were totally inhumane -- well, we were -- we were smaller than mice. Our lives weren't even as -- were not worth the life of a mouse. We had to remain lying on the ground, on concrete. There was water there, excrement -- people's excrement. In those barns -- for example, in the barn number 1, which was the one I was in in the first camp -- there were between 550 and 700 people during different periods of time. In that barn which is shut in the evening at about 5.00 and from which we are no longer allowed to depart after that time, they would bring a -- a container, recipient for -- in which we could relieve ourselves. It would fill up about one hour later. People would step over each other because the barn was full of people. These people were -- it was as if they were dead people. There was no room for you to stand. You had to stand on people, especially in the evening when it wasn't possible to see anything. And the people would have to walk around because they were ill, they were exhausted, they would have to step on each other and they would have to relieve themselves in -- in that pail. So you can imagine in the evening the excrement would reach to about 20 or 30 metres from that pail. And in the morning hours, at about 7.00 or 8.00, we would then have to clean that up. But it was impossible for us to clean that up because we didn't have anything to clean it with. We could only put it in some kind of a pail and take it out. And it remained dirty. Every day we went to do hard labour; I've already mentioned this. About 1.000 people went to do hard labour every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I think you told us in quite a lot of detail. Thank you. Judge, can I -- two other matters before I deal with the closure of Manjaca. First, you've spoken about the guards, and you described them all as military police. How were you able to distinguish military police from ordinary police?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military policemen were wearing army uniform, the olive drab uniform, camouflage uniform. I recognised this as the uniform of the Serbian army or of the former JNA, Yugoslav People's Army. I recognised military policemen on the basis of the insignia they had of the military police. They had white belts, whereas other soldiers didn't have such belts. And on these belts, there was a -- a metal buckle on which it said "military police." It was easy to distinguish them. Whereas the ordinary policemen -- that is to say, the civilian police or the Serbian police, who for some time provided security or -- or went on guard duty outside the camp, they wore blue uniforms, the blue uniforms of the civilian police. There was no difficulty in distinguishing the military from the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You say that the civilian police at some stage provided security or performed guard duty outside the camp. Do you mean you saw them?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I saw the civilian police when they came, when they arrived, and when they went on duty to provide security. And I saw them from the wire of the camp itself, I saw the positions they were occupying, the guard posts they were occupying. I could recognise many of them because the civilian police, they came to provide external security for a certain time, external security for the camp. And they would take this in turns. They were from -- one group was sent from Sanski Most, one group of Serbian policemen. I don't know if they were there for 15 days or for one month. I can't remember exactly. But before that group, the police or the Serbian policemen were from Kljuc. Later -- I don't know whether they were from Prijedor or Banja Luka, but they came again. And I know that they provided security for the external part of the camp. The camp in fact had three types of -- of wire, three different kinds of a wire fence surrounding it. Inside the camp, only the military policemen would enter the camp, go inside the camp. Between the first and second wire fence, these policemen were on duty, the Serbian policemen. And then there was the third wire fence, and that's the external fence. When I was first brought to the camp, only military policemen were present there. At the time the civilian police were not present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the civilian police take part in any of the beatings that you've described, or was it always the military police?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the whole, the military policemen were involved in the beatings and members of the army. However, in the beatings that took place at night, members of the Serbian police would also participate in them sometimes, the policemen who were providing security in the camp. In particular, the Serbian policemen from Kljuc would -- would do this. Some of my cousins from Kljuc, relatives from Kljuc, were in the camp with me and they were beaten. In the course of the night, they were taken out and both the military policemen and the civilian policemen would beat them. They were given very severe beatings with rifle butts. They were even beaten -- these civilian policemen would even hit them on the fingers with their rifle butts. They had to put their hands on the -- a table of some kind or some sort of object, and then they would hit their fingers with the rifle butts. I want to say that the policemen from Sanski Most, the civilian policemen who were there providing security, as far as I know they didn't participate in these beatings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, finally on this topic, you described the various visitors that came to the camp and the ICRC who paid visits and various, I think, international journalists and politicians. Did you ever speak to any of the internationals, either journalists or politicians who came to the camp?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you describe the regime of the camp to them as you've described them to us? In other words, the beatings, the deaths.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke to the representatives of the International Red Cross about this. But I have to say that we weren't allowed to speak about this. People were afraid to do so because the military policemen were paying attention as to whether anyone had established contact with international delegations, and they didn't allow us to establish such contact, apart from the fact that they had to allow representatives of the International Red Cross to have some kind of contact. And when the representatives of the International Red Cross came and when they entered a barn and closed the door to the barn, then the military policemen weren't allowed to enter the barn. On each occasion I spoke about the conditions in which we were living, and I asked them to get us out of there. I begged them to do so. And on one occasion, I spoke to Mr. Stojan Zupljanin and to Nenad Balaban who had come to visit the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I think you've told us about that one, and you asked about being released.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to ask you in a moment to look at a couple of videos. But before that, can we deal with the closure. I think it's right that you remained in Manjaca until December, when all the prisoners were taken out. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were some of the prisoners sent to another camp in a place called Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The day before the closing of the camp or the release of the first group from the camp, a group of 531 prisoners or persons were singled out. Their names all were called out in each barn. It was a Sunday. And they were told that they would be exchanged. They took these people to the buses that had come from Banja Luka. Since I was working in the kitchen, I was able to see the people get onto the buses. And military policemen waited for them there by the buses. They searched them. And when they got on the buses, the persons again had to bow their heads low down towards the seat. At that time I guessed that they would not be exchanged but removed in a way. I learned that that group had been transferred to another camp only on the day when I myself was transferred to the -- or transported to the Republic of Croatia, that is, the 14th of December. That was the date that I learned that the group had gone to Batkovici. I'm in fact quite sad, because some of the people I know and some of my relatives were killed in Batkovici. I know a person who was released from Manjaca due to his illness, but he waited for two days to be transported and he was killed in Batkovici. His name is Atif Dervisevic. And some other people were killed too. I just wanted to say one more thing: On several occasions before the disbanding of the camps -- of the camp, some groups had been taken ostensibly to be exchanged, but only one exchange actually took place. So people would be brought back to the camp. And then they would tell us the kind of torture and humiliation that they were exposed to during their transport to the exchange. And if you would allow me, I would like to talk merely about one transport involving persons of Croatian ethnic background who were taken to be exchanged towards Knin or, rather, towards Drnis. Their exchange lasted for three days and it failed, so they were returned to the camp. As they got onto the buses, when they were being taken to the exchange -- I mean, at Manjaca -- they had to eat salt. They had to eat a handful of salt en route there. And they were subjected to horrible humiliation. I can mention perhaps a name -- the names of a few of these people who told me that. Since the exchange did not work out, they were taken to Knin, where they were imprisoned for at least two days. The prison, or the area where they were detained, was accessible to the civilians or citizens there so that the Serbs in Knin beat them up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pause for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: She's going to say it's in Croatia. I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not having any interpretation. One moment, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No I understand the point. It's how does he know as he was in Manjaca. And I think he said already that he was told when they returned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes and he said also that he is prepared to mention some names as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My problem -- I understood what Madam Fauveau had stated, but still I'm not receiving any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I wasn't either.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because the witness often speaks -- is he speaking about what he experienced himself or something that he heard about each time he speaks about this, he should state so clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And this particular part is definitely repeating what he was told by others. And perhaps, because you will be asked to mention some names in any case later on, perhaps you could mention some names now while you are giving evidence on this particular event and that would cover -- cover the -- this part completely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just as I understand it, Judge, the -- what you're now telling us is what you were told by these men when they returned.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us the names of just some of -- not too many, but two or three of the people who experienced this.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I will. First I will mention a person of Croatian ethnic background from Sanski Most. His name is Stipe Catic, who is now currently residing in Australia. He was totally deformed because he had been physically abused so badly and so badly beaten up by Serbs in Knin, because as he told me, the prison where they were was open to them. They had access to it. He also told me that he had to eat a handful of salt en route. The temperatures were quite high, because it was in summer. I will also mention a few Croats, such as Zarko Tole, Vlado Ugrin, Ivica Zrno, Stipo Zrno. These are the people from whom I learnt about their experience on this difficult journey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps -- Ms. Korner, you may proceed with the next question. I think he's mentioned enough names.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. So you've told us that these men -- the exchange failed. Did you find out why the exchange failed?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why was that? It's the first time we've heard about -- really about these exchanges.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just remembered that they did not take Zarko Tole to be exchanged. He was a former officer of the Yugoslav People's Army of Croatian ethnic background, and he was in the camp in Manjaca, and the Croatian side sought his exchange. However, they wouldn't let him go -- I mean, the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay but the other people who were taken off to Knin but were never exchanged, did they -- were they told -- were they told what the reason was for the failure?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when they came to the place where the exchange was supposed to take place, between Knin and Drnis -- I can't remember the exact place where the location was -- where the exchange was to take place -- they had a list on the Croatian side, a list of people. And their representative called out the names of people who were supposed to get off the buses. But since Zarko Tole, who had been detained by the Serbs in the camp, didn't get off the bus, that is why the exchange failed. And the same thing happened several times. And all these people ended up in Batkovici. They were never exchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in Batkovici. I don't know what happened with them later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you were concerned, I think it's right that you went to Karlovac. And from there, did you go to Germany?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Germany, were you ill, in fact, and hospitalised?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was hospitalised in Germany for a certain period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, before I show you the video, I'd like you to look at two documents that you produced for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: These are the documents, Your Honour, that were attached to his first statement, I think. It's Attachment number 1 after the first statement. It's a list of people. If the witness could be handed the -- it's not been translated because it's just a list of people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see the -- Madam Registrar shaking her head. But in fact, I'm assured by Ms. Gustin, who's never wrong, that a whole bundle was given which contains these documents. It's marked "Attachment number 1," and it should be a list of people. Do Your Honours have this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I have all of the Attachments, Ms. Korner --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I have all the attachments, but I'm just trying to find this particular one. This is the one which is given the number --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: They've all got "77" on them, because that's the witness number. But it looks like this. It's two pages, a handwritten list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, this particular one I don't seem to have, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think Your Honours will. But I agree, there are a number of documents. And in future, it will be the rule rather than the exception that documents will be handed out as we get to them, because it is too confusing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have Attachment 6 before me, Attachment 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the simplest thing is -- perhaps I can ask the usher to be kind enough to run off -- one, two, three, four -- however many copies are required. If the interpreters haven't got it -- although I don't think they're going to need it, but ... Can I ask whether Your Honours have the next document that I want to ask him to look at, again, which is a list of people with a drawing like that. It was Attachment 5 is the -- it was split. It's Attachments 3 to 5 of the first statement, but it's in fact -- because it's a notebook, the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. Ms. Korner, I don't have that either.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Your Honour, I'll come back to that then. We can show the video. The usher when he comes back can copy that. I'm not sure why this has happened, but it can't be helped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I don't recall ever having seen that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It was attached, Your Honour would have had it with the first statement. It was attached.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As I say, Your Honour, I think it's going to be much simpler if we don't hand them out in advance and you get them when the witness gets them. When the usher comes back, perhaps he could run some copies off of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask you to look at now a couple of videos which you've already seen. The first is a video --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It was part of the video that was taken last year, Your Honour. And I think it's Prosecutor's Exhibit P447. And I wonder if that could be played for the witness to see it. Of course, the video has got to be turned on, so I wonder that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think -- where's the usher?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The usher has gone to copy, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Sir, I think you'll need to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge, I think you will need to push the "video evidence" button in order to see -- to see the video playing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Perhaps we could play that. I don't know whether the audiovisual unit had that. Video -- Prosecutor's Exhibit P447, anybody want to play it? Please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. No. I'm sorry. It was set up -- somebody has gone past --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. It was -- actually -- somebody has spun the video back to the beginning. It was actually set up at the place where I wanted it played.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll get to it. Ms. Korner, it's a short video. We've seen it already --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's not, Your Honour. We'd have to spin it right through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then let them spin it. I would be able to recognise Manjaca straight away.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. In that case, can you do it -- fast-forward, please. Your Honour, I know it's a little early. It's easier, I think, if Your Honour takes -- Thank you. All right. Can we pause for a moment. Can we go back to what we were looking at for a moment, that house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you see it on your monitor, Judge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, pause there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what are we looking at there?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the entrance to the Manjaca camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that when the Merhamet delivered clothing or whatever for people, it was put down outside the gate and the guards then went in and inspected it. Are you able to indicate here where it was put down?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. If you can roll the tape back a little bit, you can see the road leading to this place much better.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's go forwards a bit, because I saw a frame where the location was quite visible. Here, the place where the car just passed. So a truck -- a Merhamet truck would come here where the car is right now, and the packages or parcels that were sent from Banja Luka via the Merhamet were put down there, and then the military policemen would come. They opened all the parcels and searched them, taking whatever they fancied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we move the film on, then, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you want to indicate anything, if you just ask them to stop.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the entrance. Stop. Stop now. So right here, this is the precise location here at the centre. This is where the parcels would be thrown out. And after they were searched by the police, the police officers would submit a list from the camp command to the barns, and people's names were called out. The people who were on the list, they were called to get out and to pick up their parcels. They had to go out in groups with their arms behind their backs and with their heads bowed in a column, and the military police officer would take them to this place where they would take delivery of the parcel or the -- what remained of the contents of the parcel in most cases. And then they would take the parcel back to the barn. And this road to the left, this is the road that everybody used to get to the camp from Banja Luka or from the barracks, that is, 2 or 3 kilometres away from the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. That's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we move the film on, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stop. These are the premises of the military command where the police officers and military officers were accommodated, where they worked, where they interrogated us. They usually took us out in groups, and we would have to stand there for hours with our heads bowed and with our arms behind our backs next to a wall. And then they would take people in, into the corridor and then into a room where they interrogated them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, many people were beaten during the interrogations, precisely in this area, in these rooms and corridors you can see here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we move on.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are -- stop. This is the observation post where a soldier, a uniformed soldier in a military uniform was. And from that post, the soldiers were able to observe all the barns in the camp and the movements of all the people in the camp. There was also a dog house and -- or a kennel, and I also want to note that they had trained dogs between the third and the second wire fences where also the guards were. There were several trained dogs, military dogs, there. And I know that they were military dogs because conscripts trained them and fed them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Can we move on.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is where a workshop was. These are the barns.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you just pause there for a moment. Pause, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you indicate -- can we see the barn you were in in this picture or not?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that my barn was the lower one, and this barn to the left should be the upper barn in the camp. So my barn cannot be seen on -- in this frame. There were three barns in a row, and the second barn further down in the background, that's the second camp. So this is the first barn in the second camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Move on.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the entrances to the barns. You can see here. The barn consisted of three elements: These boxes to the left and to the right, and there was a concrete strip in the middle. The barns were about 60 metres or 80 metres long and 20 to 25 metres wide. Here, this part -- stop. This is an area where hay was kept in this military compound. And this area was turned into an area where meals were had. This was a makeshift kitchen, in fact. And in the left part of this area I think there were three field kitchens with wood-fired ovens that were used previously in the Yugoslav People's Army. And they were caldrons that had a capacity of perhaps 100 liters. I cannot be more specific. I don't recall whether there were one or two such caldrons in each kitchen. And food was prepared in the caldrons. And in this area where hay had been kept, there were makeshift trestle tables. And we would be taken out of the barns --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I -- we can see this on an earlier film. So don't worry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. If we could just move on.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is -- no. This is another camp. Sorry. That's another camp. Those are the other barns there. They were separated by barbed wire. There were guards there. And we had no access to that place. We were in a -- in a small area. So in two rooms, 100 by 100 metres. One of the camps had these dimensions and the other had the same dimensions. All of us were there. For a certain period of time, there were 2.500 of us. And then when people came from Prijedor and Omarska, and from other places, there were 4.000 of us --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Pause the film.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The film has gone on. But you've been describing the accommodation; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't worry about the -- the bits we've gone through, because we've been told what they are. The church we can see, is that the one that you were talking about that you were forced to build?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. This is a church which was built by the inmates of the camp. People could even recognise some of the material. For example, the copper that was used to cover the church, this had been taken -- this copper had been taken from a mosque that had been destroyed in Pudin Han in the Kljuc municipality. We built this church, and we completed it. And I can remember when the church was opened. On that occasion, a group of inmates was taken there. They were still trying to complete the church, and they were very afraid. They feared for their lives, because they were the subject of threats. They -- they were told that they would be killed there. Fortunately no one was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. That completes that film. I now want you to look, please, at a second video that was taken in August 1992, which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 468. Again, it's been set up to the place where it ought to start.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just -- I'm sorry. Could we -- could we run it back marginally. And what's happened to the sound? Go back just one shot further. There should be Christiane Amanpour standing there. Yes. Okay. Could we stop there. I don't know. Is there any sound available? Possible? Apparently not. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Pause, please, the film.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise anybody here?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can recognise this. This is the barn that I stayed in. I can recognise this man in white -- in a white T-shirt and with a moustache, he is from Gornja Sanica in Kljuc municipality. I can recognise these people, some of them here on the left. I stayed here to the left in the corner, not in the central part but right down below to the left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can see that when this newsreel was taken, all of you are sitting with your hands round your knees and your shoes off. Was this something that just happened that day, or was that a normal way you had to sit?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When a group of journalists came or camera men, that is the usual way in which we would sit. This was a -- a little later. I can also recognise this gentleman here who is standing next to the person in a white T-shirt. He is Ramiz Grapkic. I think he has from Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on. Can we move the video. Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Pause, please. Pause. No back to the wire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, I think there's no dispute that the man to the left of Paddy Ashdown as we look at him was the camp commandant, Colonel Popovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he's the camp commander, Bozidar Popovic, a JNA colonel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what fence are we now looking at? Can you tell from this?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the very entrance to the camp, the entrance for us inmates. It's the route of access for the military police, and it is on the corner behind the command. And it can be seen from the observation post. It's about -- well, between 30 and 50 metres from the observation post. That's the main entrance to the camp, to camp number 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. If we can move the film.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Stop. [Interpretation] So this is what the area looked like in the -- in the barns. You can see the earth on the ground and people lying there. They would sit there. They would lie there. That's where they stayed. Their movements were restricted. They couldn't leave those places. And this is where we spent our time. We spent all our time if we didn't go to -- to do work. We could only leave if we had to go and relieve ourselves. And on these occasions, we had to inform someone of this, and up to ten of us would have to line up and leave and relieve ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Can we move the film on, then, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "Here the prisoners live, eat, and sleep 24 hours a day. Most of these men just have arrived two days from the camp at Omarska. Their faces still haunted by memories they could not dare relate in the presence of their guard. For five minutes Paddy Ashdown was allowed to speak privately to the men."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we pause there for a moment, please. The commentator there say that is Paddy Ashdown was able to speak privately to some of the people, the men there. If private conversation was allowed -- in other words, the guards were out of earshot -- would people describe what had happened or what was happening to them?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, we were very afraid. They were observing us all the time, the military police observed us all the time. And all those who entered the camp, the military police, several of them, would accompany them, both from -- in front and from behind. It was very difficult to communicate with anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, these men apparently came from Omarska. And we've seen the -- and we're going to see another shot of the condition of those men, the -- the thinness. Were there people like that in Manjaca before the arrival of the Omarska prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were all like that. I've already said that everyone lost weight. Dozens of kilos. It's difficult to say how many exactly, but it was -- well, people would lose between 20 and 40 kilos. During the first month, I lost 26 kilos.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we move the film on, please. And if there's anything you want to say, just stay stop.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "The camp commandant had promised Mr. Ashdown total freedom to see anything he wanted."

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Stop. [Interpretation] Well, you see, we couldn't speak to anyone. The camp commander is here. And he was the one who would speak every time delegations would come in. He said that we were extremists, which was not correct. He said that we were prisoners of war, and that was not correct. We were civilians who had been taken from our houses, from our flats. People were -- were arrested in their fields. So he misrepresented us. He said, "Well, we have offered them to others, but no one wants them. No one wants to take them." And this was pure propaganda. It was a lie. I remember that he said, "Well, as you can see, the conditions they live in here are good. Our Serbian prisoners who are being held by them --" and then he mentioned Zenica -- he said that this were being held in a tunnel of some kind and said that their conditions were -- were far worse than the conditions in this camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally we wouldn't allowed -- we couldn't react to this. And just one other thing, if I may. I think that someone came from the United Nations for human rights. I don't know whether it was Mr. Mazowietsky or someone else. I can't remember right now. He came with a large group of journalists. We knew that he was supposed to come, but they brought him in around midnight. I don't know why -- why he was brought in at night like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Can we move the film.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "And he was told that wasn't possible. Even during Mr. Ashdown's visit, time was limited to a mere half hour and access was limited to a only a few prisoners. As he left, he said however bleak things seem to be, this camp did appear to be properly run. "Clearly I have had access to those prisoners without [indiscernible]. I detest their conditions. I find them deeply moving. They've had an appalling time in Omarska from where they've come from. I think it's a tremendous achievement on the part of the press to give exposure. And very probably have saved very many prisoner's lives. But every prisoner I spoke to here without the guard presence has told me the conditions were not what they want them to be but they're a hell of a lot better than what they were before. "With the visiting politician gone, what these men have suffered in the past remains largely unspoken. Caroline Tera, Manjaca prison camp in Bosnia. "Every run camp in Serbian held northern Bosnia authorities say they hold --"

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I think this is just the same film. We can stop that. Thank you. And stop the video.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was said there by Mr. Ashdown, the politician, and which I think you could probably read in the subtitles was that he was told that conditions were better than in Omarska. Did you speak to the prisoner who had come from Omarska when they arrived?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did speak to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as far as they were concerned, were conditions better here in Manjaca than in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me to draw parallel between those two camps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't --

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To compare these two camps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you compare them, because obviously you weren't at Omarska. All I want to know is did the prisoners who came from Omarska, did they tell you that they felt conditions were better here in Manjaca than in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time when they came, yes, without a doubt the conditions were better, because in Omarska there was monstrous -- monstrosities of various kinds. There were people who were killed, and we knew about this, even before this group came -- even before this group from Omarska arrived. When the journalists came to our camp for the first time, I remember that I myself and -- asked some of the journalists to go to Omarska. We asked the journalists to go to Omarska. We told them that the crimes being committed there were more serious, that people were being killed en masse over there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't want -- I'm sorry. I don't want to get sidetracked off Manjaca. But I just wanted to know. So they, as you understood it, conditions were much better than in Omarska. All right. We can now look at -- and that -- perhaps to wind up this topic, the two documents that I wanted you to look at earlier. Could you be handed first the list which is marked "Attachment 1," which will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 774, please. Now, can you tell us what that list is, Judge, first of all?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a list which was compiled in December 1992 after a first group -- the first group of inmates had been released in November -- I think that was on the 14th of November -- that's when the first group was released. And afterwards, they transferred some people from camp number 2 to camp number 1. And this is a list of the people who were transferred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From camp 2 to camp 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who compiled the list?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This list was compiled by an inmate who was on duty in the barn.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was this an official list, or was this something he just did for himself?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an internal list of the person who was on duty in the barn and who kept a record.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he provide you with a copy of that list?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Could you look at the second document, please, which were -- it's in fact three separate attachments, 3, 4, and 5. But in -- as we'll see -- And I wonder. Before they're hand --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me for just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't know if that first document P774 is both Attachment 1 and Attachment 2 or just Attachment 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. Attachment 2 seems to me to be another document very similar. But of course we don't have an explanation as yet. It's again, a list of 76 names.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that's marked "Attachment 2," so it should be seen, at least. I look at it as separate from Attachment 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So do I, Your Honour. That's just what I was inquiring about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. I think it's all part of the same document. Your Honour, it's my fault. Attachments 1 and 2 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So please, let's go ahead with Attachment 2 first before you proceed with Attachment 3, so that the witness will have a look at it and confirm to us whether this is -- in fact, from the top of the document you see that there is an indication log -- which is logo 2 to logo 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: A logo is a prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. So from camp 2 to camp 1. And this is in December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I think the two pages -- can you confirm that, please, Judge. The two pages that you were handed which have the numbers 00873151 and 152 are part and parcel of the same document. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Mr. Ackerman. I had missed the fact that there were two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So do you want them marked as together --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As Exhibit P774 consisting of two pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I doe, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay previously as Attachment 1 and Attachment 2, Madam Registrar. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And now could you be handed Attachments 3, 4, and 5.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you confirm, sir, before we look at them that these are all part of the same document which was a notebook.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. This is one document. It's a notebook. The original notebook exists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The original is where these days?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And I think -- is this right -- this was just an ordinary, as it were, school notebook, which is why we have this rather odd drawing on the front; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a notebook which the camp commander gave to the person on duty in the barn, because each barn had someone -- an inmate who was on duty. And this person would be positioned -- would -- right next to the entrance to the barn. And the camp command would establish contact through this person. So the person on duty would be given an empty notebook of this kind in which he was to keep records on the inmates in the barn.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, it's almost half past 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm just going to finish --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Whenever it's convenient for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm just going to finish this, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this contains records for which barn and at what period?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These records were compiled by Zukic Zikret who was on duty in the barn in which I was detained. This was in camp number 1. The records were brought up to date with the situation on the 14th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we just then quickly look at one page, the beginning of Attachment 3, the B's. We see number 59 crossed through and some writing. What does that mean? I think it's Besirevic. Mesud.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mesud Besirevic, number 59 it's been crossed through. And there was is a note that says he was exchanged on the 31st of October, 1992. I know Mesud Besirevic. He is someone from Sanski Most. And I know that he was exchanged in Vlasic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if we look at the page with the number 00873155 under D's, I think we see your name and other Draganovics.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Under number 132 you can see my name and the registration number of the International Red Cross, which is 200.729. And below you can see the names of some of my relatives from Kljuc, Kemal Draganovic, Hasan Draganovic, Muharem Draganovic, Muslia Draganovic. They were in my barn.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was your relative Muslia exchanged on the 14th of November, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wasn't exchanged. He was released then, because on the 14th of November, 1992 -- was that the date? Yes, I think it was. He was released with the first group, and he was moved to the Republic of Croatia to Karlovac in Croatia. At the moment, he is in Switzerland.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that would then be convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a 30-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Judge, I think you returned to Sanski Most in October of 1995, the 15th of October.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that very close on the heels of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina when they retook the town?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Republika Srpska army had gone, had left Sanski Most, and the BH army took control of Sanski Most, the entire territory, except for a small portion of the territory of the municipality of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So between 1992 and 1995, did Sanski Most remain under the control of the Republika Srpska authorities?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you told us, you were immediately almost reappointed as a judge. And did you take part thereafter in a number of investigations into the events that had taken place?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, my mandate as a judge never ceased in the period between 1992 and 1995, because officially I continued to be the judge and, in fact, the President of the court, since I was elected by the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, the Serbian authorities removed me from the court illegally, and then they unlawfully arrested me and tortured me in the camp, and they also destroyed my property. The same happened to thousands of non-Serbs, Bosniaks and Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Now, I wanted to deal, please, with -- in various separate topics your investigations. First of all, did you personally go to buildings which had been occupied by members of the SDS officials and army?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
