utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to move, please, to other aspects of your investigations. And I want to start with the declarations of death that were issued by the Sanski Most court. I think you provided to the Office of the Prosecutor a copy of what's called "The law on administrative procedure."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we've got copies -- we think that was omitted so we've got copies here. Only -- the only part which has been translated is relevant to this issue. I mean, it's a huge book, as Your Honours can imagine. And Your Honour, we do -- we do actually have the book here. I mean, it's not -- I mean, not in court. But it's actually -- if anybody needs it, it's in the possession of the evidence unit. But a photocopy has just been produced. And if the witness can have, please -- the Defence should have it, because it was attached to one of the statements. There are enough copies, if you want it. It was attached to Attachment 1 to the statement of June 2000.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to correct you. This is a law on out-of-court proceedings. This is a law which is in force. And on the basis of this law, we conducted proceedings in order to declare that missing people were dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Can we just look very quickly at the relevant part. If you could turn to Article 60 --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which is where the translation starts, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- Which states that is "in the procedure of declaring missing persons dead and proving death, the Court will decide on declaring missing persons dead and on the proof of death." And then in Article 61, it sets out which individuals may be declared dead upon application to the Court. Then we see that for someone who's been missing for five years and who's over 60, someone who's been no reports over five years and is likely no longer to be living, individuals who disappear in what could be described by -- what is described by insurers as acts of God, shipwreck, traffic accident, et cetera, for six months. And then item 4, "an individual who disappeared in a war or in relation to events of war and about whose existence there have been no reports a year after the cessation of animosities." Now, Judge, was that the section that was applied to people who were missing as a result of the events between 1992 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I know the procedure is set out, but it's probably quicker if you just describe to us the procedure and then we'll look at an example of one of the documents. If someone had been missing and wished to obtain a declaration of death, what was the procedure that had to be followed?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the proposal to declare someone dead was usually submitted by members of the nuclear family, by a spouse or by children. If the missing person was not married or had no children, then the parents would submit this proposal to the Court. Upon receiving this proposal -- and the birth certificate had to be attached to the proposal, the birth certificate of the missing person in question, and other evidence would also be suggested. Usually these were witnesses who knew something about the disappearance of the missing person. In such cases, the judge would then schedule a hearing, at which he would take a statement from those submitting the proposal and then would carry out an investigation, would examine the registry of births and deaths and other document if they had been attached to the proposal. The judge would then question the witnesses, if witnesses had been suggested. If the witnesses could confirm that someone had been killed and confirm that this information was reliable, if they could confirm that the missing person had been killed at some location, and if the Court considered these facts to have been determined, it would then take a decision in which it would declare that this person died on a certain date and at a certain location. If there was no information or no witnesses to -- who could testify that the person had died, then the Court would publish an announcement in official papers in which it would ask for -- anyone who had any information to provide the Court with this information about the missing person. And after the legal period had expired, the Court would issue a decision in which it would declare this person to be dead -- or rather, missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Korner. Judge, just a simple clarification. I see that the text of this law in the Serbian language and in Cyrillic script was published in Sarajevo in 1989. And we're now talking of 1995. Did this law -- this particular law get any -- get amended in the meantime between 1989 and 1995, or was it identical as we see it in -- in the document that you have before you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This law was adopted in 1992, and its validity was extended in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in -- I think what the learned Judge wants to know -- in 1995, was that the law that was applied and thereafter?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With no amendments to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, there's a schedule that's been prepared and given to my learned friends of all the declarations of death that were issued, which we will just be asking to be produced. If there's no dispute about this procedure, I don't propose to go into any further details other than look at one example. Perhaps I could just be assisted on this from the Defence. Is this procedure in any way the subject of dispute, or is it going to be disputed that these declarations of death were lawfully and properly issued? That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't think disputed would describe anything that I'm going to do. I may ask some questions about it. But I think "disputed" probably doesn't describe it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with what Mr. Ackerman has said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you know what to do, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we just look, Judge, please, at one example of these -- these declarations of death that you were issued -- that you were issuing, which - if I can find my own copy - sorry, Your Honour. I filed everything. Because I filed it so carefully that I -- Yes. These were not attached. They're documents which I hope Your Honours have got. They were marked 9.6 in the disclosure, 9.7. And they were handed in. There was a bundle -- it looks like this. A small bundle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if the witness could have, again, please, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What number does it have, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 9.7, which is the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And 9.6 -- no. Sorry. 9.7 is a birth certificate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. That's exactly the -- it's a birth certificate.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. And 9.6 is one of the rulings. I see Mr. Ackerman is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't know -- I don't know where to find these, Your Honour. I may have them, but I don't believe I have them here. I don't know when they were given to me or how they were given to me or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have had them for quite some time now. That's a day or two before the witness started giving evidence three weeks ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Well, Your Honour, with the Defence we simply --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: With a list. We supplied them with a list. And this was handed out -- whenever it was. It says 9.6 -- 9.7, 9.6. We can put it on the ELMO, and we'll supply Mr. Ackerman with a copy -- with another copy if he can't find it. Could we put up first, please, the 9.6, which is headed "Municipal court in Sanski Most, 20th of October, 1997," and if the witness could be given the B/C/S version. Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this an example of one of your -- the rulings which relates to a gentleman named Muhamed Smajlovic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is. This is a decision of the municipal court in Sanski Most, which bears the number 714 through 97. And it was issued on the 20th of October, 1997 at a hearing which was held on that date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just so we can see the procedure, the -- if we go to -- if we could move it up to "statement of reasons." And if we could move the statement of reasons slightly up. Yes. The Court heard -- it says, "Ruling on the proposal.." The Court heard the proposed witnesses and inspected the attached birth certificate of Muhamed Smajlovic. It heard witnesses who said that Mr. Smajlovic was taken away from Kotor Varos by what's described as Serbo-Chetnik military units with other villages to the hospital and killed there. And there are -- there's a various description of what had happened, that the bodies having been buried had been dug up and incinerated in the saw mill in Kotor Varos. And then the -- over the next page, we can see that the Court decided that it was established. And the judge on this case -- not yourself, but Judge Ahmet Tatarevic -- certified the death. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the second document -- if we can just put that up -- I think is the birth certificate -- or a copy of the birth certificate of the person who was declared dead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if it helps Mr. Ackerman, they were disclosed to the Defence on the 18th of May of last year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Korner, may I ask you to explain to the Court what are you seeking to prove with document 9.6 and 9.7.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're showing part of the evidence which we say goes to genocide is the large number of people who were killed during the course of these events. That's why we're leading the exhumation evidence and the declarations of death. We've alleged thousands of people were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So this is part of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Yes, thank you. Your Honour, could, I think, both documents be made the same exhibit, just to keep them together, which will be 779 -- perhaps 779.1 can be the -- the birth certificate, because it's 9.6; and 779.2 -- 779.2, rather, will be the ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I think we have -- yes, exactly. The extract from the law on administrative procedure has not been given a number.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And 7 --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. Then P779 will be the law on administrative procedure; 780.1 and .2, the documents just described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me ask the witness a question with regard to this particular procedure that he was describing or referring to earlier. Do I understand you well, Judge, that this is a -- these are proceedings before a special court, the nature of which is non-contentious, a court of non-contentious jurisdiction, in other words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a regular court, and the procedure was regular. But the proceedings were called "out-of-court proceedings" because we have a law on out-of-court proceedings in which -- according to which certain legal relations -- certain legal issues are dealt with on the basis of that law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And the other question is: In these proceedings, is the state -- the -- in particular, the registry office where the office responsible for the archiving and registering of civil acts -- is any -- is this office represented in the course of these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I haven't understood your question very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is why I asked you whether it's a court of non-contentious jurisdiction. A court of contentious jurisdiction is when there are two opposing parties fighting a claim. And a court of non-contentious jurisdiction is where there is only one party asking for a remedy or for a measure from that particular court. Now, these, I understand, are proceedings in which there's only one party. But what I am asking you now is whether in these proceedings the interests of the Registry of civil acts is represented. In other words, whether there is anyone who was consulted or who has a say in the course of these proceedings from the administration side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you've understood that quite correctly. These are legal proceedings which involves only one party. We don't have two parties with opposing interests. The person submitting the proposal must prove that it is of legal interest to establish certain facts in the out-of-court proceedings. And in these proceedings, the Court obtains certain evidence, such as this certificate here -- such as this birth certificate. This certificate was taken from the Registry of Births and relates to the person who is in question in the proceedings. When the Court takes a decision, it sends this decision to the office in order for it to be implemented. It take it to the registry office so that the date of death can be listed in the registry office and that person can be declared dead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But in the course of the proceedings, that registry office, does it have a say in the proceedings? Is there a measure of control reserved for the administration during the proceedings. In other words -- or is it just the judge hearing the evidence brought forward by the party filing the application and that's it, with -- without any possibility of control from the office which ultimately is responsible for the archiving of these civil acts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The registry office doesn't have the right to participate in the proceedings, but the Court does cooperate with the registry office. If the registry office has something it wants to object to or if it doesn't agree with some of the personal details of the missing person, in such cases the registry office can officially request that the Court make corrections, that the Court correct certain information. But the registry office doesn't have the right to make amendments of any kind in the Court's decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And my last question to you is: Once an application is filed for a certificate of death to be issued by the Court, is the application itself given publicity? In other words, is -- does it become something that the general public can be made aware of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's enough. Ms. Korner, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Okay. Those documents can be taken off, please?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh. If those documents can be taken away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before I move on, there's one set of documents that I want to ask you about that you found. You told us a long time ago that when you were arrested in Sanski Most on the 25th of May, one of the people who was -- who was involved in your arrest was a man named Dane Kajtez.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you to look, please, at a set of documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, they were disclosure 4.197 in that small bundle. The Defence they were disclosed to on the 10th of November of the year 2000. But I'll have them put it up on the ELMO in case people don't have them here with them. And I'd like to take these documents in order but produce them as one exhibit, which I'll do at the end. There are -- Could the first one be handed, please, a report of the lower court investigating judge Sanski Most. And if the witness could get the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, the documents that I have -- I have one document which is, I suppose, what you are referring to now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And it is 4.197.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With the other number 01106755.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then however I have another document with the same number, 4.197.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do they form the same document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. They're separate documents but they relate to the same issue that I'm about to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And that Your Honour will hear about. Your Honours, can I just check that Your Honours then also have a document headed "41 --" sorry, "4914."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then "182."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All of those relate to exactly the same incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But we now have up the report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This -- although it's headed "The lower court investigating judge Sanski Most," I think was dealt with at a time -- we can see November 1992. If you turn the report over, to the other side of it - yes - 9th of November, 1992. Do you know who Dr. Ljiljana Prosic was -- is?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. She is a doctor. At the time she was employed in a healthcare institution in Sanski Most. That was the Sanski Most healthcare centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this report by her in November of 1992 deals with the killing of nine people from the village of Skrgevita is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kruhare.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. But the killing was in Kruhare. But did the persons come from the other village named?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Skrgevita.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this document and the next documents we're going to look at documents that you recovered?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honours, I can say this relates to a particular killing on the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, it describes the people who were killed and the injuries to them. These people who were killed, do you know what ethnicity they were?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The nine persons, the nine unfortunate persons listed here were of Croatian ethnicity. They were from the village of Skrljevita.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Can we, then, move, please, to the next document that's also got the disclosure number 4197. The number at the top is 01103365. Now, if we look at the B/C/S version, it appears -- it's a handwritten document. And it's signed, if we look at the end -- could you tell us what the signature says.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the signature of Kajtez Dane, Danilusko. That's his letter to -- the letter he wrote in the Banja Luka prison to Vlado Vrkes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, can we take, first of all, that in stages. Who found that letter and where was it found?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found this letter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was it found?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it in the premises of the SDS, of their municipal board, in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just remind us again. Who was Vlado Vrkes?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vlado Vrkes was together with Rasula, the president of the SDS. He was the vice-president or the vice chairman of the Crisis Staff. And for a time he was the chairman of the executive board of the Serbian municipality of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Can we just look briefly at the contents of this letter. He had been arrested apparently and explained about his wife coming there. And then in the third part, the third paragraph, he says: "I can't take this endless and painful investigation any longer. You are all supposedly working on my behalf, but in fact, nothing is happening and you don't give a damn, you just care for yourselves." Next paragraph: "Why didn't you go to see Maric, the Court President, he could have sorted all this out and set us free, but you say, "let Dane serve his sentence for a while, it's good for him." Do you know who Maric was, who's described as the court President?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if Maric was the President of the court, but I do know other persons who are mentioned here in this letter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. We're going to come to the others. All right. Then it goes on: "Vlado, you know as well as the rest of you, what and how much I have done for that damned Sanski Most. There is no need to waste words on it, but it's worth mentioning. What I'm about to say to you ... is a very serious matter ... don't take this as a threat or blackmail, because that is not my intention. My intention is to get out of here as I deserve or for someone to join me behind bars. You know that at Manjaca, I and a few others liquidated 12 people on two occasions, which was ordered and witnessed by inspector Vujanic, Mico Krunic, who was the warden of the Betonirka prison at the time, Mile and other inspectors. The chief at that time was Vrucinic." I'm just going to read the next paragraph and then I'm going to ask you about this. "I'm going to file charges against myself in court because I was only a Serbian soldier and executioner who liquidated people on orders issued by the people named there and by you too, Vlado." All right. Now, he talks about liquidating 12 people at Manjaca. Do you know to what incident he refers there?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. Two groups of six persons each were liquidated. I assumed that they were liquidated because they were singled out from the transport at Manjaca and returned. The first group consisting of six persons was returned on the 6th of June. The second group was returned on the 12th of June. And it's a total of 12 persons. Those people were never found again. They were Bosniak Muslims from Sanski Most. So they were in the transport. They were being transferred from Betonirka and from Hasan Kikic school, the gym there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, he refers to an inspector Vujanic. Do you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. That's Drago Vujanic. He is a lawyer. He went to school with me, and we also studied together. He worked in the Serbian police. He was the chief of the service in the public security station in Sanski Most. He led the groups to Manjaca, and he brought the list. He was the one who took me away. Right now he is in Banja Luka, and he holds an important job in Banja Luka. He is still in the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the next man, Mico Krunic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Mico Krunic very well. He was a retired police officer, a Serb. He was a very active member of the SDS as a retired police officer. In April he was mobilised again, and he joined the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't -- I'm sorry to interrupt. I don't need too much details about him. But was he at the time, as this letter suggests, in charge of Betonirka prison?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know who he's referring to by the nickname Mile -- or the name Mile?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that person. That's Mile Dobrijevic nicknamed Mima. He was a crime investigations inspector in the public security station in Sanski Most. When the war stopped and after the Dayton Peace Agreement was signed, he has been the chief of the public security station in Ostra Luka, which is called the Serbian Sanski Most. On several occasions, he led groups to Manjaca. I saw him. He interrogated me at Manjaca. He took part in the beating -- the beatings of people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, Vrucinic. Was he the chief of police at Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the chief of the public security station in Sanski Most. Tomo Delic is also mentioned here. You left that name out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I haven't got to the next paragraph. I'm going to read the next paragraph. The next paragraph says: "As for this charge against me, the gist of my defence will be that we went hunting and were attacked. If I get a harsh sentence, in other words, if you fail to get me out of here, I will say that I killed on orders issued by Tomo Delic and Vlado Vrkes, with the intention of resettling the village of Skrgevita as soon as possible. All of which could be -- I'm sorry. All of which could easily be proven in court." Tomo Delic is the man that you told us about at some length, I think, earlier on in your evidence; is that right? A member of the Crisis Staff and the SOS.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. And he was in the command of the 4th Battalion of the 6th Krajina Brigade. And together with Nedeljko Anicic, he was the chief coordinator and the strategist of the planning for the military formations and for the taking of the territory in the Sanski Most municipality -- I mean, in military terms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Then if we just go on -- I think I can summarise most of the rest of it. He's -- he then goes on to say: "If I have to be held responsible and serve my sentence, I don't have to be the only one from Sana to do so when there are so many people and great Serbs around. Why would I have to bear the entire burden myself, why would I have to be the guinea pig? So, I am going to defend myself by any means and implicate you in this, so that you can serve your time as well, because I was not the one who started this war, I didn't issue the orders or hold any function." And finally, he ends up by saying: "As soon as I give this statement in my defence, the investigation will have to be reopened and you won't be able to remain at large." And then in the P.S.: "Go to Talic, Mladic, Karadzic, to whoever you can think of, but get me out of here. Don't just say that if the sentence turns out to be harsh, we'll get it reduced -- we'll get it reduced it -- I think translation has gone wrong somewhere -- or I'll be granted an amnesty because I don't believe that, nor do I have any more faith, nerves or patience. My fellow prisoners here, from various towns, who also killed the balija and the Ustasha, are being acquitted and helped by their municipalities. Only Dane is being put into deep shit by his own side. So be it, Serb gentlemen." Now, can we look at the final documents on this particular incident. Could we look, please, at 49 -- 4.914, which is a report by someone called Predrag Lazic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if that could go up on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That, I think, dated the 7th of December, 1992, Command of the 6th Krajina Brigade of the military police Sanski Most. It says there was this murder and alleges four people were responsible, including Mr. Kajtez. There was an investigation, and weapons were seized. And the Banja Luka CSB confirmed by phone there's an entry cartridge matching the light machine-gun taken from Dane Kajtez being found at the site of the murder. The aforementioned persons have been apprehended and processed, and will be taken to the Banja Luka military remand prison. Does the name Predrag Lazic mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Predrag Lazic was a member of the military state security service -- Serbian state security service or the national military state security, as they called it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the final document -- really it's a bit repetitive. But it's the list of criminal reports. Could that -- 4.182. That's a list of the criminal reports from December the 5th 1992 until February of 1993. And the second refers to the same incident and lists the people again. And I don't think we need -- and it says that all -- at the back of that page, "All the said criminal reports were submitted to the office of the public prosecutor."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Then, Your Honour, may those documents become P781.1 through to .4 in the order that I've produced them,.1,.2,.3,.4.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally this, Judge: Do you know what happened to Kajtez? If you don't know, say so straight away.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to or what I have been able to see from the documents, I have been able to establish that Dane Kajtez had been released from prison and that he had returned to Sanski Most and that he had been given a Bosniak cafe in Sanski Most in the very centre of the town. I know that he changed his name by applying to the police authorities in Sanski Most as early as in 1993. I saw the decision on the change of name. It was issued by the public security station in Sanski Most, the Serbian public security station. And it was also entered in the registry office in Sanski Most, in the relevant registries. I think that this Tribunal also has this decision -- a copy of this decision. I learnt that Dane Kajtez had killed more than a hundred people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where is he now? Do you know? I mean, is he alive, as far as you're aware?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he is alive. He is somewhere in Serbia. I can't tell you the exact location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm going to finish this all. I've just got two more questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your investigations, was he ever prosecuted, brought to trial or serve any sentence? I'll rephrase that, because that's three questions rolled into one. First of all, we see that a prosecution was launched in respect of these murders. Do you know whether or not a trial ever took place?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say he was released and by 1993 he was applying for a change of name.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in fact, there will be other evidence from the military court records that we've obtained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Korner. We'll break for another 30 minutes, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I recognise Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like about five or seven or eight minutes at the end just to discuss a couple of matters --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- That are responding to your request, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Responding?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Responding to a request made by you last week. I just have some answers for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, there's one matter I need to raise as well. But that will take all of 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you moderate --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Half past 1.00, would Your Honours think?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. I think that should be enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I would do is I think I'll deal with other documents that he's covered and then go on with the exhumations tomorrow morning, because that, I think, is a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Judge, I want to come to another similar document relating to an investigation that you recovered. It's the document with the disclosure number 4.184. Again, it was in that small little extra bundle.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I wonder if the judge could be given -- and we'll put up the English on the ELMO. Now, if we could put the English up on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was an investigation apparently carried out by the security service centre in Banja Luka -- or rather, by Sanski Most into the murder in the village of Hrustovo -- Hrustovo -- I've always had some difficulty with this one -- and some photographs that were taken. And photograph 1 --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm afraid that if Your Honour looks at -- that is really all the copies were photocopies and the originals are not much better -- the original photocopies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Photo 1, house owned by Husko Merdanovic in the village of Hrustovo, in the garage of which a charred corps was found. And then the garage, a broader view, and the state of the charred corpse. If we go over to the next document, please, the lower court of Sanski Most, 23rd of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Can we just -- sorry. Yes. The document -- could you pull the document -- you've got the bottom half of the document on. I want the top half first. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Police station Sanski Most. Enclosed with these documents, we are sending you an investigation report written on the 10th of April, 1993 following the discovery of a charred body in the village of Hrustovo." And that's signed, investigating judge, Milena Zoric. Did you know her?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Milena Zoric was a judge of the municipal court in Sanski Most while I was still the president of the court. She remained there as a judge after I had left while Serbian authorities were present in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we see that the report of the pathologist and the investigating judge after the discovery of the corpse and then the description of the -- what was found. And at the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we go to the next page, please, usher, on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can see after the investigation -- yes, that paragraph at the bottom. If you'll just pull that up slightly. Thanks. And according to the knowledge of those present, the house is most probably the property of Huska Merdanovic of Hrustovo. And after completing the investigation, the investigating judge told the workers to bury the said corpse, and so on and so forth. And then, as I say, we can see the unfortunately completely unidentified photographs. Now, again, Judge, was this a document that you found in the court files at Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a document I found in the court files in Sanski Most. If I may, I would just mention something briefly. Merdanovic Husko, his fact is -- his name is in fact Husein from Hrustovo. He was killed on the 31st of May, 1992. In that same garage, 29 people were killed, 29 Bosniaks: Nine children, women too, and Huska was among them in that very same garage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I just mention, Your Honour -- this results -- Your Honour will recall that I told Your Honour about difficulty with witnesses coming. May I say that those difficulties have been resolved. The witnesses will be coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Both of them?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Both -- not not the one that Madam Fauveau didn't require.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Relating to one of them --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Relating to one of them, there is our decision 92 --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which was made conditional on the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly. When I say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On the other witness being here to give evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly. The other witness is now coming, and there's a second witness related to that who wasn't the problem -- or was also actually a problem but who deals with the discovery of the bodies. So -- but I thought I'd mention that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. It's important, Ms. Korner. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. If that could be made Exhibit 782, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I now look at some other documents that you recovered, please. Could you be handed the document marked 41012. That's a document --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Excuse me. I think the 782 has been used.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What was 782 then according to your records?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: In the transcript, page 71, line 12. 785? P785.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. According to -- according to the sequence that I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. No. According to the sequence that I have, the documents 4.197 -- and there were two documents with that number, the first one with disclosure number 01103365 and 01106755, together with documents 4.914 and 4.182 have together become Exhibit P781.1 to.4.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly. So I don't have a 782 anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that was the last exhibit that was tendered.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this new one, 4.184 with the photos that no one can make heads or tails of would in fact be 782. Definitely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is, Ms. Korner, while we are discussing this, I still have from this bundle a lone document which is a certificate of -- or decision certifying the death of certain --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Begic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mesud Begic, a decision given by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And this has not been used as of yet, has it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, it hasn't. I mean, I looked at it on the break, and it doesn't seem to me that other than he had signed it, as opposed to another judge, that it didn't add anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But I just wanted to know whether it's going to be tendered as an exhibit or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour. At the moment, I don't think so. I'll recheck that for tomorrow morning. But I don't think we need that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I'd like -- you've now got, have you, 4.1012. That's a document dated the 27th of October from the security centre Banja Luka, addressed to the Sanski Most public security station, the SJB. And we can summarise it. It's an order to subordinate -- well, perhaps we should just read the first part. "Pursuant to a request from the first -- from the command of the 1st Krajina Corps of the army of Republika Srpska to engage 158 members of the police from Banja Luka CSB region, who will be resubordinated to the 1st KK command, to execute designated tasks in Jajce." And it shows that there are to be 34 policemen and one senior employee from Sanski Most. And if we look at the next page -- it's your page, the same page but for yours it's the next page -- it's signed by Stojan Zupljanin, the centre chief. Do you know where that came from? I'm sorry. Did you find that yourself, I should ask.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from where did you -- where did you find that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The public security station in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the next --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honour, could that be made Exhibit 783. Your Honour, I'm just checking to make sure I know which one ... [Microphone not activated] I'm sorry, Your Honours. [Microphone not activated] Your Honour, I think I'll come back because --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not entirely sure that they put this on the list, so I may have to come back to that tomorrow. So I'll move directly to the exhumation evidence. Oh actually, there's one more thing that I can do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- I want you to look, please, at a set of transcripts which were attached to the statement of October 2000. And they're right at the back of the big bundle. They've got "7.77" on them. And the translation numbers begin 019007754. Now, I think you told us when you were last testifying, Judge, that there were various broadcasts that you heard on Serb radio. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In which there was propaganda broadcast and also demands for the surrender of weapons.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you provide to the Office of the Prosecutor in October of 2000 when you were seen by investigator Kellie Ward two audiotapes containing broadcasts from Sanski Most radio?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I gave those two audiotapes to the Office of the Prosecutor. That's a direct record of the Serbian radio which was made when Sanski Most was attacked -- on the day when Sanski Most was attacked. Obviously the propaganda which was being carried out was terrible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say that at a later stage we're going to have a witness present who was actually on these recordings. So it will just take up time to listen to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we just look, for example, at an example of -- these were transcribed. If you take -- you've got the B/C/S version -- the one that begins with the page number 01104873 in the B/C/S, and in the translation 01907754. And do we see there an announcer stating that there's a meeting at the Tomina school and that persons from Kamicak, Kljevci, and Sanica to come to a meeting there, to bring lists of the former Muslim units, lists of arms in the villages legal and illegal, lists of arms and military equipment, the full names of leaders and their extremist groups and their locations. "We repeat that your villages are surrounded and that you wouldn't have a chance in an open armed conflict. That is why we warn you to come to the meeting without fail, because by doing that you will prevent the destruction of property and people for which you will held -- you will be held responsible before the people. Your failure to come to the arranged meeting will be understood as acceptance of armed conflict which is what you will get. The Command of the Serbian Armed Forces. Since the representatives of the above-listed villages have failed to come -- have failed to come to the arranged meeting, meaning they have accepted war ...." And then there's a female announcer: "Muslim and Croatian ethnicity of Vrhpolje, Hrustovo, Capalj, Kamicak, Donja Sanica, Biljani, Priesijek, and Budimlje. As well as all of the hamlets around these villages which have not handed over their weapons, to hand them over to the nearest military unit straight away. Any resistance and opening of fire on the members of the Army of the vernz Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina will provoke an armed attack on that village, resulting in great material damage and human casualties for you. You do not have a chance in armed combat, so keep a cool head. Collect the arms and take them to the nearest military unit ...."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just seeing if there's any others that I want to go through. I think not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just before we make these an exhibit, Judge, can you tell us, who recorded -- how did you collect these audiotapes? Who recorded the material?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to say something briefly. While I was in prison --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just object to him always wanting to answer something that's not asked him and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But let's hear what he has to say first. Maybe it's relevant, Mr. Ackerman. If it's not, I will stop him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He wants to say when I was in prison. He was asked who recorded the tapes, and he wants to tell you a story about when he was in prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But he may be revealing some information that might be relevant. I don't know a priori.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's difficult to tell who's the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know. You are right. The witness tends to go at a tangent sometimes. But in the meantime, I still have to wait and see what he has to say first.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, I have to say it's normally relevant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this relating to these broadcasts, Judge?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you can tell us what you'd like to say about when you were in prison.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of the Serbian radio of Sanski Most -- I heard this being broadcast throughout the day on the 27th of May. Do you understand? This is what I want to say. In prison we listened to Sanski Most radio, because it comes from the command, which is in the building of the prison. These words could be heard. That's just what I wanted to say. And this is exactly what we could hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the question was: Who recorded these transmissions?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you get the tapes from?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got these tapes while I was in Germany. I got them from a gentleman who had been given these tapes. He gave them to me. I could provide you with his name, but -- I don't know. His name is not important. What is important is the person who recorded it. I know that Mr. Husto Jakupovic recorded this. Unfortunately he has died. He was a Bosniak who was involved in education and he was at home in Sanski Most at the time. He is the person who recorded this tape, and this is something that he confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, may that, then, be made Prosecutor's Exhibit 784 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to the transcripts of a tape that has not had any kind of a reasonable foundation laid for it. As far as we know, this tape was created by actors in Germany. I mean, there's no evidence that this was actually a broadcast of the radio that was recorded other than just the purest and most unidentified form of hearsay. I think that requires some more authentication that what we've heard so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge -- Judge, have you listened to these tapes? Have they been played back to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Several times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And are you in a position to confirm here on oath or with your solemn declaration that this is a faithful recording of what you heard or what you said you heard while you were in prison.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am ready to take an oath and to swear that this is what I heard and that this is the original text of the broadcasts made over the Serbian radio at the time when Sanski Most was attacked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So do you still maintain your objection, Mr. Ackerman, at this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour he heard it -- I understood that he had heard the Sanski Most radio but not that he was saying that he heard these particular --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. No. This is why I asked him. I mean ... So let's leave it at that. And I think, Ms. Korner, unless you have any further questions on this particular --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There's a second set of transcripts and tapes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Do you want to continue now? Because we had agreed to stop at half past, so that you can bring up --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Pick up tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Thank you. So I think the witness can be escorted. Judge, you know -- you are aware that you have to come again tomorrow and the subsequent two days at least. You will tender this as an exhibit tomorrow morning, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Your Honour. I've asked if I can tender it as Prosecutor's Exhibit 784.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now I have lost the page. Okay. Thank you. Thank you, Judge. You may withdraw, and we will meet again tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, while Your Honours -- if Your Honours have still got it there, just to show that this is clearly authentic. If Your Honour looks at page 5 of the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You see a name at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He's being called as a witness to talk about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see. Page 6 -- page 5, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Page 5 at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, you had asked us to report to you on two matters. I think you asked on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The first of those was the status of the defendant Brdjanin exhibits. We have worked on those. We're in contact with Ms. Chuqing Chen regarding those. I think we have almost got the problem solved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There will be a point where I might want to formally offer some that haven't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That will not be a problem, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You also asked about the Banja Luka 92 bis situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I reviewed what was available to me in that regard that I could find. There are three outstanding Banja Luka 92 bis matters that I am aware of: 7.118, [Realtime transcript read in error "7.168"] 7.167, and I think it's 2.4, the deceased witness. On January 17, 1992 I filed an objection as to 7.118 and 7.160 and indicated I had no objection regarding the deceased witness. I requested that 7.118 and 7.167 be made available for cross-examination. The Prosecution responded to that objection the next day. On 30 January, the Chamber issued its decision not to admit 7.167 and to admit 7.118 after certain redactions from it had been made by the Prosecution. So as I understand at this point we are waiting for the Prosecution to make the redactions ordered on 30 January 2002 by the Chamber and that the matter regarding the deceased witness, 2.4, was deferred until a later time at the request of, I think, both the Prosecutor and Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I recall there was an agreement to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the transcript reflects that I said 7.168 at the beginning, and what I really said was 7.167. The outstanding matters are 7.118, 7.167, and the deceased witness, 7.167 having already been ruled by this Court not to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm afraid, Your Honour, that I -- I know that Your Honour raised it on Friday, and I intended to have a look at it, and Your Honours' legal officer raised it this morning, but I think I'll have to go back and have a look. I can't remember who all these witnesses are now, except for the one who's dead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Please do, Ms. Korner, for a very simple reason that I tried to explain to you --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour did. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before without saying too much, the legal officer -- my legal officer who's working on Banja Luka will soon be leaving the team.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And she is anxious, and so am I, to have all the documents -- first make sure that they have been given an exhibit number, which is not the case for some of the 92 bis statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And secondly, there is still this -- these two outstanding matters that Mr. Ackerman has referred to following our decision of -- I don't recall the date -- but our decision on 92 bis that need -- need to be attended to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I'm -- I've been told - and I thought that was right - that when Your Honour made a ruling, that we'd have to call 7.167. I think we informed the Chamber -- I can't remember -- or shortly afterwards we weren't going to bother. I recall that we were made -- made redactions. So I don't think there is anything outstanding other than to make the redactions requested and to give them exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think the -- the transcript did not get the numbers correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It won't be the first time and it won't be the last time, I can assure you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just want to make sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 7.118 -- now I've lost it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 7.118 is the one that's awaiting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- redaction by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The Chamber ruled 7.167 not be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, correct. And the Prosecution, in any case --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And 2.4 is outstanding. That's the deceased witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There was a 7.160 I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That was included in our decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And I believe that that witness may have been called already.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. We called -- that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. So that witness has actually been here and testified.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's, in fact, Your Honour -- I think the easiest thing is to go back to Your Honours' decision and to do a double-check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I will definitely inform Your Honours tomorrow morning what the situation is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Korner. I thank you. So tomorrow morning we will continue with Witness 7.77.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, there's one matter I need to raise that's quite short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour will recall that Mr. Dzonlic, the lawyer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- provided copies of the letters which were relating to the termination of employment as a result of ARK Crisis Staff decision. They were handed over to Mr. Ackerman I believe a couple of weeks or so ago now. I'm only concerned with this: I don't -- I'm not going to produce them myself - because the witness gave oral testimony to that effect - unless it's still challenged, in which case I need to produce the letters as exhibits. I'm just not anxious to add to the exhibits in this list. So I wonder if I just could be told whether there's now any challenge to that part of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, very frankly, Your Honour, I haven't had a chance to have them translated into English so that I can understand what they say, either orally or in writing. It's just one of those things that I kind of put aside and didn't get to yet, but I will get to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman. And then we will decide. There are various options, actually, depending on what the outcome will be.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, Your Honour, the simplest thing would be to produce them. But I mean, which is adding exhibits unnecessarily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. And then if they all say the same thing in particular, I mean, we only need one or two.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understood from what you told us when you reported again on the matter that there was a variation on the same thing; in other words, that there were some which said one thing one way and others which said the same thing in another way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. There are -- as I recall the instructions I've been given, there are two sets, as it were. There's one that says "pursuant to --" I say one. There are about seven that say "pursuant to a decision of the ARK Crisis Staff dated," and then others which say "because you haven't reported for work for five days or whatever, you're dismissed."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So please, Mr. Ackerman, do give this your early attention. I think with that we can adjourn. Tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you.
